"It was too easy," Lieutenant Miller said, his voice barely a whisper over the drone of the Hudson's engines. "No patrols, no searchlights, not even a stray dog barking. It doesn't feel right."

"War is never right," Jacques replied, his gaze fixed on the silent man huddled in the corner of the fuselage. "But you are correct. The rendezvous was quiet. Too quiet for my liking."

"Quiet?" a new voice cut in, sharp and authoritative. "I'd call it a perfect execution of a plan, gentlemen."

Miller and Jacques spun around. Major Strickland, whom they'd believed to be in London, was stepping out of the forward navigator's compartment. He held a steaming mug in one hand and his face was set in a grim, tired mask.

"Major, sir!" Miller stammered. "We didn't know you were aboard!"

"There's a great deal you didn't know, Lieutenant," Strickland said, his eyes flicking to their silent passenger. "You two have been wondering why the Gestapo practically rolled out a red carpet for you tonight. You assumed we had a leak, that you were walking into a trap, didn't you?"

"The thought crossed my mind, sir," Jacques admitted. "When the pickup signal came a full five minutes early, I was certain we were finished."

"Exactly," the major nodded. "And that's precisely what I was counting on. Not a leak on our side, but on theirs. We've known for a month that the head of the Gestapo in Amiens has been feeding false information to his superiors in Berlin. He's ambitious. He wants to catch the infamous 'Le Corbeau' himself and present him as a gift to the Reich."

The major took a sip from his mug and stared at the two young men. "So we gave him what he wanted. We fed his informant a trail of breadcrumbs leading directly to this field, tonight. We made him believe he was one step ahead of everyone. While he had all his men waiting for a trap to spring on you, the real Le Corbeau was being put on a fishing trawler out of Dieppe."

Miller's jaw hung open. "You mean to say, sir, that this whole flight, the risk, it was all a distraction?"

"A vital distraction," Strickland corrected him. "And a test. We had to know if the Amiens Gestapo's information channels were truly compromised. Your 'easy' mission tonight proved they are. We drew their eyes to the sky while our real asset slipped away by the sea."

"But, sir," Miller protested, gesturing toward their passenger, who hadn't moved a muscle. "What about him? Who is he?"

For the first time, a flicker of something other than weariness showed in the Major's eyes. It might have been pity. "He is a baker from a village outside Lyon. A brave man who volunteered. His family is already safe in Switzerland. To the Germans who will debrief their failed agents, he is Le Corbeau, slipped through their fingers. His capture, or his escape, it didn't matter. Only that he was the focus."

A heavy silence fell in the cabin, broken only by the hum of the engines. It was Jacques who broke it, his voice low and troubled.

"But Major, what if they are not fooled? What if this is the trap, after all? They let us take this man, they let us fly away, so that they can follow us? So they can find our base?"

Major Strickland's face hardened again into a granite slab. "That is the question, isn't it? The one that keeps an old man like me awake at night. It's the gamble we take every single time. We have to assume they are as clever as we are, and then be one step cleverer."

"So what's the answer, sir?" Miller asked, leaning forward. "What's the next step?"

"The next step?" the major said, a thin, humorless smile touching his lips. "The next step is that we are not flying to England. We have enough fuel to make it to the coast of neutral Spain. We will land at a prearranged strip, and we will wait. If no uninvited guests show up on our tail within twelve hours, we will know the deception was a success. If they do show up--"

The major let the sentence hang in the air, the implication as cold and vast as the night outside.

"Well," Miller said, trying to force a casual tone, "I've never been to Spain. I hear the weather is--"

He never finished. From the cockpit, the co-pilot's voice crackled through the intercom, sharp with alarm. "Major, you'd better get up here! There are two of them, sir! Unidentified aircraft, closing fast from the stern!"

Colonel Welsh was already on his feet, his face a granite mask, one hand braced against the fuselage. "Pilot! Report!" he barked toward the front of the plane, his voice cutting through the sudden chaos.

The intercom crackled to life, but it wasn't the calm voice of a moment ago. This was strained, tight, and laced with an urgency that sent a fresh chill down Dawson's spine. "Engine fire! Starboard engine is on fire! Trying to feather the prop now!"

The rhythmic thrum of the two Wright Cyclone engines he had grown so accustomed to was gone, replaced by the desperate, straining roar of the single port engine and the terrifying whoosh of the flames being fed by the high-speed wind.

The pilot’s voice, tight with strain, came crackling back. "The fire suppression system isn't responding, Colonel! We're trying to feather it, but she's burning hard! I'm cutting fuel to the starboard side. Stand by!"

Dawson, a pilot to his bones, could feel it in the pit of his stomach. They were losing altitude, the one good engine fighting a losing war to keep them in the sky with the dead weight and drag of the other. He exchanged a quick, grim look with Freddy, and the same thought was mirrored in the English youth's eyes. They were in the middle of the Atlantic Ocean, at night, with a crippled bomber that was fast becoming a glider made of lead.

We're past the point of no return for the Azores, and Casablanca is still over a thousand miles away. We can't maintain altitude on one engine, not with this load. Sir, we have maybe fifteen minutes of flight left. Twenty if the pilot is a magician."

Colonel Welsh absorbed the news without a flicker of expression. He turned from the cockpit door and his gaze fell on the briefcase still sitting on the table. For a long moment, he just looked at it. Then he looked at Dawson and Farmer.

"The little item of fate, sir," Dawson said, his voice barely a whisper. "The tiny little something you were talking about."

The colonel nodded slowly, a deep, world-weary sigh escaping his lips. "Yes, Dawson. It seems fate decided to deal us a hand after all." He straightened up, the moment of reflection gone, replaced by the sharp-edged focus of a commander. "All right. We're not going to sit here and wait for the ocean to come to us. We're going to ditch. Pilot, what's your assessment for a water landing?"

"It'll be rough, sir," the pilot's voice came back, devoid of any emotion now. Pure professionalism. "Darkness is the main problem. No horizon. Now."

Make sure the raft deployment isn't fouled. And Dawson," he added, picking up the briefcase and holding it tight against his chest, "this does not leave my side. If we go down and I don't come up, you forget about me and you find this. It must not be recovered by anyone else. Understood?"

"Yes, sir!" Dawson said, his mind snapping into focus. The time for shock was over. Now was the time for training, for instinct, for survival.

He and Freddy moved with the grim efficiency of men who had faced death in the sky before, though never quite like this. They pulled the bulky yellow life vests from their stowage compartment and wrestled them on, pulling the straps tight. The air in the cabin was growing thicker with smoke, and the angle of the deck was becoming more pronounced. Dawson could hear the rest of the crew moving about in the forward sections of the plane, their voices clipped and professional as they ran through the ditching checklist.

"Hatch is clear, sir," Freddy reported, his hands running over the emergency exit's locking mechanism.

"Good man," the colonel said. He had wedged himself into a corner, his back against the bulkhead, the briefcase clutched in his lap. His eyes were closed, but Dawson knew he wasn't praying. He was thinking, calculating, planning even now, at the edge of disaster.

Every few seconds, a powerful shudder would wrack the fuselage as another piece of the burning engine tore away into the night. It was a strange and terrifying feeling, to be inside a machine that was actively tearing itself apart around you.

"Five minutes!" the pilot's voice blared from the intercom, jolting them. "We're at five thousand feet! Going to try and level out just above the waves!"

"This is it, then," Freddy said quietly, his knuckles white where he gripped a support strut.

"Looks that way," Dawson replied, trying to sound braver than he felt. He thought of his original mission, of the sealed envelopes he and Freddy had destroyed. He thought of the President, flying this same route in a different plane. This decoy mission, designed to test for information leaks, had run into the one thing no spy-master could ever account for. A simple, catastrophic mechanical failure. A crazy little twist of fate.

"Two minutes! Landing lights are on!"

The plane leveled out, the single engine roaring as the pilot fought to slow their descent. Through the window, Dawson could see the reflection of their own fire on the black, churning water below. The waves looked like mountains of ink.

The world dissolved into a cataclysm of noise and violence.

There was a colossal, ear-splitting shriek as the bomber's belly met the surface of the Atlantic. The impact was not a crash so much as a series of brutal, bone-jarring collisions. The plane skipped once, twice, and then the nose dug in. The deceleration was so immense it felt like hitting a solid wall. Dawson was slammed forward, the webbing cutting into his hands. He heard a sharp crack, the sound of metal bending and snapping, and then the ocean came for them.

A wall of black, freezing water exploded through the side of the fuselage where the wing had been. The cabin was plunged into absolute darkness and chaos. Dawson was torn from his handhold and sent tumbling, disoriented, his lungs screaming for air he couldn't find. "Freddy!" he yelled into the darkness, his voice raw. "Colonel!"

"Here!" a voice choked out nearby. It was Freddy. "I'm here, Dave! Are you all right?"

"I think so! Where's the colonel?"

"Dawson!" The colonel's voice was weaker, but steady. "I'm here. The hatch. Get the hatch open, now! We're going down fast!"

"It's jammed!" he yelled.

"Together!" Freddy shouted, appearing beside him in the gloom.

They both threw their weight against the lever. With a groan of tortured metal, it gave way. The hatch swung open, and the cold night air and the roar of the ocean filled the space. A sliver of moonlight illuminated a terrifying scene. The B-25 was broken, its back snapped, the starboard wing completely gone. The nose was already underwater, and the tail was rising high into the air. They had seconds.

"Out! Everybody out!" Colonel Welsh ordered. "Get the raft!"

Freddy scrambled through the hatch first, pulling the cord for the inflatable raft stowed just outside. With a loud hiss, the yellow craft began to bloom to life on the surface of the churning water. Dawson clambered out after him, turning to help the colonel. The senior officer was moving slowly, his face etched with pain. He was still clutching the briefcase.

"My leg," he gasped. "Think it's broken."

"We've got you, sir," Dawson said. He and Freddy grabbed the colonel under his arms and hauled him through the opening just as the tail of the plane began its final, fatal slide beneath the waves. They half-pushed, half-threw him toward the raft. Freddy was already in it, pulling the colonel aboard.

"Dave, come on!" he yelled.

Dawson was about to jump when he heard a cry from the front of the wreckage. "Help! Over here!"

It was the pilot. He was clinging to a piece of the shattered cockpit window frame, his co-pilot floating unconscious in his vest beside him.

"Hang on!" Dawson shouted. He didn't think. He swam the few yards to them, the icy water seeping into his bones. He grabbed the co-pilot's vest and started kicking back toward the raft. The pilot, one arm clearly broken, followed, using his good arm to swim.

It was a nightmare of a struggle. The waves were high, and the wreckage was sinking with a terrible sucking sound, threatening to pull them all down with it. But somehow, with Freddy pulling from inside the raft and Dawson pushing from the water, they managed to get all four of them aboard. The navigator and the radio operator were gone.

They paddled furiously away from the sinking bomber. A moment later, with a final gurgle and a rush of bubbles, the B-25 vanished beneath the surface, taking its fire and its secrets with it.

Silence fell. A profound, overwhelming silence, broken only by the slap of waves against the thin rubber of the raft and the ragged, gasping breaths of the five survivors. They were a tiny, insignificant speck of yellow in a universe of black water and distant, indifferent stars.

Dawson lay on the floor of the raft, exhausted, shivering uncontrollably. He looked at Freddy, whose face was a pale oval in the moonlight. He looked at the injured pilot and the unconscious co-pilot. Finally, his eyes settled on Colonel Welsh. The Chief of all U. S. Intelligence was propped against the side of the raft, his injured leg stretched out before him. In his lap, held securely in both hands, was the wet, battered briefcase.

After a long time, the colonel spoke, his voice quiet but clear in the vast emptiness of the night.

"Well, gentlemen," he said, staring out at the endless, heaving ocean. "The enemy has not learned of the President's plan." He paused, and a grim, humorless smile touched his lips. "And now, neither has anyone else. The orders are at the bottom of the Atlantic, and so are we. The board is wiped clean."

Freddy Farmer found his voice. "So what do we do now, sir?"

Colonel Welsh gave the Yank air ace a sharp look, and then nodded his head. "Now, Farmer? We do what any good Intelligence man does when his primary plan has been utterly destroyed by a twist of fate." He adjusted his grip on the briefcase, as if to reassure himself of its weight. "We survive. And we wait for another."

Dawson's hand trembled as he took the signal pistol. The plane drew nearer, a low drone now audible over the waves. It was flying low, on a search pattern. A big, four-engined bomber. His heart leaped. It had the distinctive twin-tail of a B-24 Liberator. An American plane.
"It's one of ours!" Freddy shouted, unable to contain his excitement. "A Liberator!"
"Wait," the colonel commanded, his hand on Dawson's arm. "Let him get closer. We only have a few flares. We have to make sure he's in a position to see us."
The Liberator droned on, its path set to pass about a mile to the south of them. It was close, but in the vastness of the ocean, a small black raft could easily be missed.

A crewman was visible in the waist gunner's window, waving. The Liberator waggled its wings in acknowledgement and then began to circle again, climbing to gain altitude, its radio operator no doubt sending their position back to base.

"You'll be traveling under new identities," the colonel explained. "We're flying out of here in two hours. A transport will take us to the outskirts of Casablanca. From there, you will proceed into the city. You'll be assigned new papers, new names. You'll be two American civilian engineers, attached to the Army Corps of Engineers, helping with port reconstruction. A perfect cover."

"And what will we be doing there, sir?" Freddy asked, his voice a mix of apprehension and excitement.

"You'll be my eyes and ears," Colonel Welsh said, his voice dropping. "Casablanca is crawling with spies. Vichy French, German Abwehr, neutral opportunists. They'll all be talking about this great Nazi victory. I want you to listen. Mingle in the cafes, the bars. Find out what the word is on the street. I want to know what the enemy's intelligence network is saying. I want to know what their next move is. They've sprung their trap, and now I want to know if they're smart enough to check if they've actually caught anything."

He stood up and looked from Dawson to Farmer, his gaze piercing. "This isn't about flying. It isn't about dogfights. It's about being patient, about watching, and about listening. One wrong word, one careless move, and you'll not only get yourselves killed, you could compromise the entire Allied high command. Do you think you can handle that?"

Dawson's heart was pounding. Just yesterday he was a pilot, concerned with altitude, air speed, and enemy fighters. Now he was being asked to become a spy in one of the most dangerous cities in the world. He looked at Freddy, who had a determined glint in his eye.

"We can, sir," Dawson said, his voice firm.

"We won't let you down, Colonel," Freddy added.

"Good," Colonel Welsh said with a nod. "Because the fate of this conference, and perhaps a great deal more, may depend on how well two young air aces can play the part of civilian engineers." He walked to the door and paused. "Get some rest. A car will be here in ninety minutes. Your new lives begin today."

"You next, Farmer," the colonel ordered.

"After you, sir," the English youth replied.

"That's an order!" Welsh snapped, and Freddy, knowing better than to argue, allowed himself to be pulled aboard.

"Easy there, Lieutenant," the sailor said kindly. "We've got you."

We need to let the enemy believe their lie for as long as it is useful to us, without letting that same lie destroy us from within."

"How can a lie like that be useful, sir?" Freddy asked, frowning in confusion.

"Think about it, Farmer," the colonel said, a flicker of something like excitement in his tired eyes. "The Nazis think they have decapitated the American government and military. They think they've won the intelligence war. They will grow cocky. They might relax their guard in other areas. They might move assets based on this false information. If we play this right, we can use their 'greatest victory' to set a trap for them that will dwarf anything they thought they'd achieved."

Dawson stared at the colonel in awe. The man's mind was a thing of wonder. Stranded in a life raft only hours ago, he was already plotting a counter-move on a global scale.

"So our new mission, sir," Dawson said slowly, "is to help you play this out?"

"Your new mission," Colonel Welsh corrected him, "is to stay alive and follow my orders to the letter. This is no longer a simple flying job. You're in the real intelligence game now. It's a dirty, dangerous game, and the rules change every minute. You did well in the air. Now we'll see how you do on the ground."

The rest of the flight passed in a blur of exhaustion. The corpsman gave them blankets and some bland biscuits, and Dawson, despite the turmoil in his mind, drifted into a fitful, dream-haunted sleep. He awoke with a start when the PBY's engines changed their pitch for landing. He looked out the window and saw the lights of a sprawling coastal base twinkling in the darkness below. They had made it. They were back on solid ground.

The landing was smooth. As soon as the flying boat was moored, an ambulance and a jeep were waiting for them. The injured men, including a heavily sedated Sergeant Corrigan, were carefully transferred to the ambulance.

Await my return. Do you understand?"

"Yes, sir," Dawson said.

"We're not prisoners, Freddy," Dawson said, walking over to the single window. He could see the silhouettes of palm trees against the night sky. "We're evidence."

He splashed cold water on his face from the basin, the simple act feeling like a luxury. He looked at his reflection in the small, cracked mirror. His face was gaunt, his eyes bloodshot, with a new hardness in them that hadn't been there two days ago. He had been a pilot. Now, Colonel Welsh had told him, he was in the real intelligence game. He wondered if he was ready for it.

Finally, close to dawn, the key turned in the lock. The door opened and Colonel Welsh stepped inside. He looked even more exhausted than before, but his eyes were sharp and alert.

"All right," he said, closing the door behind him. "I've spoken with the base commander, and more importantly, I've been in contact with Washington."

Dawson and Freddy were on their feet instantly. "What's the word, sir?" Dawson asked eagerly.

The colonel allowed himself a thin, weary smile. "The President is safe, of course. He's been diverted to an alternate route. The plan is proceeding. My signal got through without any leaks."

"And the news of the crash, sir?" Freddy asked. "What are they saying back home?"

"That's the delicate part," Welsh said. He sat on the edge of the empty cot, the first sign of physical fatigue he had allowed himself to show. "For now, the official story is simply that a transport plane is overdue on a transatlantic flight. There's no mention of the President. But the Nazi propaganda machine has already started. Their broadcasts are claiming they've shot down Roosevelt's personal aircraft. They're calling it a turning point in the war."

"The colossal nerve of them!" Freddy exclaimed.

"Let them," the colonel said quietly. "Washington has decided to let them run with it, for now. It serves our purpose. While they're celebrating, the real conference can proceed without a hitch. The President will arrive in Casablanca, meet with Churchill, and be gone before the Germans even realize they've been had."

"So we just sit here and wait, sir?" Dawson asked.

"No," the colonel said, shaking his head. "We don't. We have a new assignment. Washington agrees with my assessment. The enemy's belief that they've won gives us an opportunity. We're going to use it."

He paused, letting his words sink in. "The original plan was for us to fly to Casablanca. We're going to stick to that plan. You two are going to Casablanca."

Dawson blinked. "But, sir, how? We can't just stroll into the city. What if someone recognizes us? What about von Steuben's people?"

"You'll be traveling under new identities," the colonel explained. "We're flying out of here in two hours. A transport will take us to the outskirts of Casablanca. From there, you will proceed into the city. You'll be assigned new papers, new names. You'll be two American civilian engineers, attached to the Army Corps of Engineers, helping with port reconstruction. A perfect cover."

"And what will we be doing there, sir?" Freddy asked, his voice a mix of apprehension and excitement.

"You'll be my eyes and ears," Colonel Welsh said, his voice dropping. "Casablanca is crawling with spies. Vichy French, German Abwehr, neutral opportunists. They'll all be talking about this great Nazi victory. I want you to listen. Mingle in the cafes, the bars. Find out what the word is on the street. I want to know what the enemy's intelligence network is saying. I want to know what their next move is. They've sprung their trap, and now I want to know if they're smart enough to check if they've actually caught anything."

He stood up and looked from Dawson to Farmer, his gaze piercing. "This isn't about flying. It isn't about dogfights. It's about being patient, about watching, and about listening. One wrong word, one careless move, and you'll not only get yourselves killed, you could compromise the entire Allied high command. Do you think you can handle that?"

Dawson's heart was pounding. Just yesterday he was a pilot, concerned with altitude, air speed, and enemy fighters. Now he was being asked to become a spy in one of the most dangerous cities in the world. He looked at Freddy, who had a determined glint in his eye.

"We can, sir," Dawson said, his voice firm.

"We won't let you down, Colonel," Freddy added.

"Good," Colonel Welsh said with a nod. "Because the fate of this conference, and perhaps a great deal more, may depend on how well two young air aces can play the part of civilian engineers." He walked to the door and paused. "Get some rest. A car will be here in ninety minutes. Your new lives begin today."

"And he's the man getting the credit," Freddy added, a grim edge to his voice. "They're all celebrating. They completely believe it. They think they've won."

"Can I help you, gentlemen?" he asked, his tone weary.
Dawson stepped forward. "Yes, sir," he said, keeping his voice respectful but professional. "We've come to inquire about the new pilings for Pier Four."
Mr. Abernathy's tired eyes sharpened instantly. The weariness vanished, replaced by a keen, appraising intelligence. He looked from Dawson to Freddy and back again.
"Ah, yes," he said, his voice dropping slightly. "The shipment from Baltimore has been delayed."
The code was complete.
"Step into my office," Abernathy said, holding the door open. "We seem to be having all sorts of supply chain issues these days."
The office was cluttered with maps and shipping manifests. Abernathy closed the door securely behind them.
"Colonel Welsh sent word you were coming," he said, his voice now crisp and efficient. "Report."
Dawson quickly recounted their experience at the Brasserie Lorraine, focusing on the mood of the patrons and the specific information they had overheard.
"They're completely convinced, sir," Dawson concluded. "They're toasting the Luftwaffe and a man named Major Kleist, who they say is the Abwehr chief here."
Abernathy nodded slowly, absorbing the information. "Kleist. Yes, we know of him. He's very good, and very dangerous. The fact that they're naming him publicly is a sign of their supreme confidence. They believe they've dealt a mortal blow."
"So what's our next move, sir?" Freddy asked.
Abernathy tapped a pencil on his desk, his brow furrowed in thought. "For now, you've done well. You've confirmed the enemy's state of mind. That's vital. I will relay this to the Colonel. Your orders are to continue as planned. Establish your cover. Be seen. Be the boring American engineers you're supposed to be. But keep your ears open. Kleist's people will be everywhere, and they'll be arrogant. Arrogant people make mistakes."
He stood up, signaling the end of the meeting. "Go back to your hotel. Tomorrow, actually go down to the port. Ask questions about dredging. Make yourselves known to the foremen. Live your cover. I'll get a message to you if you're needed. Otherwise, our next meeting will be in three days. Same time, same place."
As they left the consulate and walked back into the chaotic streets of Casablanca, Dawson felt a strange mix of exhilaration and dread. They had passed their first test. They had gathered their first piece of intelligence. But Mr. Abernathy's words echoed in his mind. Major Kleist was very good, and very dangerous. And he and Freddy were now operating in the man's backyard. The game had just begun.

The air grew thick with the sounds of a thousand conversations in French, Arabic, and Spanish, the bleating of goats, the honking of ancient horns, and the distant clang of work being done at the port.

He wasn't looking at them, but Dawson felt a prickle of certainty that their little performance had been duly noted and dismissed. The German, if that's what he was, was paying them no mind. "We're aware of that," Dawson said, pulling a notebook from his pocket as if to make a note. "That's why we're here. We need to see the existing plans, and take our own soundings."

The foreman seemed about to argue further when a black Citroën sedan pulled up nearby, scattering a flock of seagulls. Two uniformed Vichy policemen got out, followed by a man in a pale grey suit. It was the man with the monocle.

He didn't so much as glance at the foreman or his crew. His cold, pale blue eye fixed directly on Dawson and Freddy. The monocle seemed to magnify the intensity of his gaze. He stood there for a long moment, an unlit cigarette held between his fingers, simply observing them. The entire dock seemed to fall silent around them. The foreman and his men froze, their eyes downcast.

Dawson's heart hammered against his ribs. This was it. This was the test. He forced himself to hold the man's gaze for a second, give a slight, indifferent nod as one might to any stranger, and then deliberately turn his attention back to the foreman.

"As I was saying," Dawson continued, his voice miraculously steady, "we'll need access to the harbormaster's office. Where would we find him?"

He could feel the German's stare boring into him. Out of the corner of his eye, he saw Freddy squinting out at the water, looking for all the world like an engineer contemplating the tide. It was a masterful piece of acting.

The foreman, however, was terrified. He swallowed hard and stammered, "The harbormaster... his office is in the main administration building. At the end of the quay."

"Thank you," Dawson said crisply, closing his notebook. "We'll be back tomorrow to begin our survey."

The man in the grey suit finally broke his gaze. He said something in sharp, guttural German to one of the policemen, then turned and got back into the car. The Citroën drove away, its tires crunching on the gravel.

As soon as it was gone, the tension on the pier broke. The foreman wiped a sleeve across his sweaty brow. He looked at Dawson and Freddy with a new expression, a mixture of fear and something that might have been respect.

"You are either very brave or very foolish, you Americans," he whispered, his voice hoarse.

"We're engineers," Dawson repeated, his own throat dry. "We have a job to do. That man has nothing to do with us."

The foreman looked over his shoulder, as if to make sure the car was truly gone. He leaned in closer. "That man," he said, his voice barely audible, "is Major Kleist of the Abwehr. He is the most dangerous man in Casablanca. For your own good, you should do your job and then go home. This is not a healthy place for Americans right now."

With that, he turned his back on them and began shouting orders at his men, the conversation clearly over.

Dawson and Freddy walked away, their footsteps echoing on the wooden planks. They didn't speak until they were well away from the pier, lost in the throng of people near the port's main gate.

"Major Kleist," Freddy said, his usual cheerfulness completely gone. "So we've met the famous Abwehr chief already."

"And he's met us," Dawson added grimly. "Abernathy was right. He's very good. And he's very dangerous. He wanted to see us. To size us up for himself."

"Do you think he bought our act?" Freddy asked.

"I don't know," Dawson admitted, hailing a taxi. "I honestly don't know. We did what we were told. We acted the part. But that look he gave us... it wasn't idle curiosity. He was filing us away. He was putting our faces in his memory."

They rode back to the hotel in silence. The morning's success at establishing their cover now felt hollow. They hadn't just been seen, they had been scrutinized by the one man they had been sent to deceive. The game had suddenly become infinitely more complicated. They had walked into the lion's den, and the lion had looked them right in the eye. Now all they could do was wait, and wonder when he would decide to pounce.
